3-1.title: What Is Energy?
3-1.learn:
KEY IDEAS

Energy is the ability to do work or cause change. Two important kinds are:
- Kinetic energy = the energy of MOTION. Anything moving has kinetic energy.
- Potential energy = STORED energy because of an object's position or condition (like a ball at the top of a hill, or a stretched rubber band).

What changes kinetic energy: MORE mass and MORE speed both give MORE kinetic energy. Of the two, speed has an especially strong effect.

Example 1 — Ball on a hill
A ball at the top of a hill has potential energy (stored, because of its high position). As it rolls down, that potential energy changes into kinetic energy (motion).

Example 2 — Compare kinetic energy
A fast-moving truck has more kinetic energy than a slow bike, both because the truck has more mass AND because more speed adds kinetic energy.

Example 3 — Stretched band
A stretched rubber band stores potential energy. When released, that stored energy becomes kinetic energy as the band snaps.

3-2.title: Forms of Energy
3-2.learn:
KEY IDEAS

Energy comes in many forms, and all of them can do work and change from one form to another:
- Mechanical energy: the energy of moving objects (and stored motion energy).
- Thermal energy: from moving particles; gives us heat.
- Chemical energy: stored in food, fuel, and batteries.
- Electrical energy: from moving electric charges.
- Light energy: travels as light (radiant energy).
- Sound energy: travels as vibrations you can hear.

Example 1 — Match the form
A battery stores CHEMICAL energy. A moving bicycle has MECHANICAL energy. A glowing bulb gives off LIGHT energy. A ringing bell makes SOUND energy.

Example 2 — Heat source
The warmth from a campfire is THERMAL energy, which comes from fast-moving particles.

Example 3 — Food fuels you
The food you eat holds CHEMICAL energy that your body uses to move (mechanical) and stay warm (thermal).

3-3.title: Energy Transformations and Conservation
3-3.learn:
KEY IDEAS

An energy transformation is when energy changes from one form into another. Energy is constantly being transformed all around us.

The Law of Conservation of Energy says energy is NEVER created or destroyed — it only changes form. So the total amount of energy always stays the same.

Example 1 — Flashlight
A flashlight changes CHEMICAL energy (battery) into ELECTRICAL energy, then into LIGHT energy (and a little thermal energy).

Example 2 — Roller coaster
At the top of a hill the car has POTENTIAL energy. As it speeds downhill, that potential energy transforms into KINETIC energy.

Example 3 — Conservation
If a toy car starts with 100 units of energy, it still has 100 units total afterward — some may have become heat or sound, but no energy was destroyed; it just changed form.
